text: Last lesson you read one file. This time we bring in both real files this dataset ships with — the trip records and a zone lookup table — and start actually reshaping data with select, filter, and withColumn.

header=True tells Spark the first row is column names, not data, and inferSchema=True has it scan the file to guess real types, like treating LocationID as an integer, instead of defaulting everything to a string.

select narrows down to just the columns you actually need, which is cheaper than carrying every column through every later step. filter keeps only matching rows — and when you combine two conditions, you need the ampersand and pipe symbols, not Python's plain and or or, because each side is a column expression evaluated per row.

Both of these reference the same column, but col with a string name isn't tied to one specific DataFrame variable. That flexibility matters the moment you're combining columns from two different DataFrames — exactly what the joins in the next lesson require.

withColumn takes a name and an expression. If that name already exists it replaces the column, otherwise it adds a new one — here, deriving fare per mile from two columns you already have. This is the real-world shape of most transform logic in a pipeline.

Real trip records sometimes have a missing passenger count. isNull finds those rows, na.drop removes rows missing a required field entirely, and na.fill substitutes a sensible default instead — which one's right depends on the field.

Once you can explain why combining filter conditions needs the ampersand instead of Python's and, and the difference between na.drop and na.fill, you're ready for Lesson 46, where we aggregate this data and join it to real zone names.
